t: Maximum Length of Subarray With Positive Product - Track Signs, Not Values
o:
## Understanding the problem

We need the longest contiguous subarray whose product is positive. A product's sign is decided by exactly two things: whether a zero appears (product 0, never positive) and the parity of the count of negative numbers. Magnitudes are irrelevant, which is lucky because values up to 10^9 would overflow if multiplied naively.

In `[1,-2,-3,4]` there are two negatives and no zero, so the entire array of length 4 qualifies. In `[0,1,-2,-3,-4]` the zero acts as a wall; the right segment `[1,-2,-3,-4]` contains three negatives, so we must trim down to an even-negative window, and `[1,-2,-3]` achieves length 3. In `[-1,-2,-3,0,1]` the left segment again has three negatives, and dropping the prefix through the first negative leaves `[-2,-3]` of length 2.

With n up to 100000, quadratic scanning is on the edge and a single linear pass with constant state is the natural target.
k: A product's sign depends only on zero-occurrence and the parity of negatives, so track sign lengths instead of multiplying values.
Zeros are hard walls: every candidate subarray lives strictly between two zeros.
A window holding an odd number of negatives becomes positive by trimming the prefix up to its first negative or the suffix from its last negative.

a.n: Approach 1: Brute Force Over Every Start
a.i: Fix a left endpoint and extend the right endpoint while maintaining a running sign that flips whenever a negative enters and dies at any zero. Record the longest stretch whose sign stays positive. This translates the statement literally and is hard to get wrong, but every element is rescanned once per start, giving quadratic worst-case work.
s: Extend j from i onward, breaking immediately at a zero.
Flip a sign variable for each negative number encountered.
Whenever the sign is positive, update the answer with j - i + 1.
a.t: O(n^2) - each of the n starts may rescan to the end of the array.
a.sp: O(1) - only a sign flag and the answer are stored.

a.i: Cut the array at every zero and process each zero-free segment independently. If a segment holds an even number of negatives, the whole segment qualifies. Otherwise exactly one negative must be excluded: dropping the prefix through the first negative or the suffix from the last negative are the only two candidates worth checking, and the longer survivor wins.
s: Walk the array, buffering elements between zeros.
When a zero (or the end) is hit, evaluate the buffered segment.
Count its negatives; if even, its full length competes for the answer.
If odd, find the first and last negative positions and take the better of the two trims.
a.t: O(n) - every element is appended to and read from a segment once.
a.sp: O(n) - the current zero-free segment is buffered.

a.i: Keep two rolling counters: pos, the length of the longest positive-product subarray ending here, and neg, the same for negative product. A positive number extends both counters; a negative swaps their roles before extending; a zero resets both to nothing. The answer is the running maximum of pos, and everything fits in two integers.
s: On a zero, reset pos = neg = 0.
On a positive value, pos grows by 1 and neg grows by 1 only if it was nonzero.
On a negative value, swap: the new pos is old neg + 1 (if old neg was alive) and the new neg is old pos + 1.
a.t: O(n) - a single pass with constant work per element.
a.sp: O(1) - two rolling counters and the answer.

w: Use the one-pass sign DP in an interview: it is short, O(n) time, O(1) space, and easy to prove. Common pitfalls: letting a zero participate in a window (it must reset both counters), forgetting that a negative swaps the roles of the two lengths, and multiplying actual values (overflow risk in fixed-width languages). Edge cases worth testing: all zeros, a single element, and inputs whose best window is empty (answer 0). Likely follow-ups: report the subarray indices themselves, or solve the streaming variant where only constant state may be kept.
